speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to introduce a motion on a question of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that the Assisted Home Ownership Program announced by the Minister of Urban Affairs grants substantial subsidies to builders of rental housing and that low income people are by this very fact at the mercy of builders and owners of such accommodation who are really the ones that benefit from such a program, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That this House recommend to the minister to amend the Assisted Home Ownership Program by providing the payment of subsidies for low rents to tenants with a modest income so that they may be able to rent in the building of their choice thanks to the additional income this subsidy will represent. This measure will make low income people the true beneficiaries of the assisted rental program.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that I had discovered certain facts in relation to the Dorval lease, and I put them on the record. I find that among the tenders which were received three appeared for final consideration, and those three varied from one level of guarantee to another level of rate. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: DAIRY POLICY-REASON FOR IMPORTATION OF DAIRY PRODUCTS-POSSIBILITY OF REDUCTION OF SUBSIDY
speechtext: The hon. member's question, his explanation of it, is at fault. What the dairy farmers of Canada actually have done has been to increase their production more than the amount of money we have to pay them for subsidy. They can continue to produce if they wish, but they will not get the subsidy on it. They will not get any more money than I have. subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-ACCESS TO TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON CORPORATE CONCENTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which relates to the activities and reports of the Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration which began its hearings in the city of Ottawa on Monday. At the time the commission was set up, we in the New Democratic Party said that it was not necessary, that what was really required was government legislation on the question of corporate power. However, in good faith we made a submission on Monday to that commission.
As a result of the attitude taken by the commissioners, a good part of which horrified the members of our party in terms of the restrictive view that they had of their own task, we requested at the earliest possible instance a transcript of the proceedings of that day to form our own judgment as to what was said in precise detail, so we could
November 5, 1975

therefore take appropriate political action during the last couple of days in this House of Commons. However, we were informed by the commission that it was not possible to supply a transcript until Friday of this week.
At the same time, we were referred to Nethercut and Company, a private firm engaged in providing technical assistance in the production of transcripts, and they too said that such transcript could not be made available until Friday. We were prepared to accept that on the assumption that this ruling would hold for all members of parliament. However, I learned today that a transcript was provided to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), or at least to the Prime Minister's office, this morning, some two days ahead of the time that it would be made available to other members of parliament.
As a member of this House, I submit that this infringes upon not only my rights and privileges as a member but also those of all members who may well have wanted to respond as we do in what we regard as a responsible and political way. I repeat that the transcript has been made available to the Prime Minister but has not been made available to other members of the House. Therefore, if Your Honour decides that I have a prima facie case of privilege, I will move that this matter be referred immediately to the House committee on privileges and elections.

subtopic: MR. RODRIGUEZ-COST OF TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON CORPORATE CONCENTRATION
MR. RODRIGUEZ-COST OF TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON CORPORATE CONCENTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I believe affects all members of this House and is relevant to the issue raised by my leader. As we are all aware, earlier this year the government established a royal commission to investigate corporate concentration in Canada. This commission has begun its hearings and I telephoned the commission this morning to request the minutes of its hearings. I was told that the minutes would cost 25 cents per page and would only be available after a week. I also understand that the commission will not be making copies of the many briefs presented to it available to members of this House, and is instead suggesting that people presenting the briefs should spend the money to make them available.
These hearings are extremely important to members of parliament for many reasons, but primarily to enable us to evaluate whether the exercise is worth the expenditure by the government, and secondly to gain any information which might become available on Canada's power structure. It is vital that the members of this parliament have rapid access to this sort of information if we are to be able to determine the quality of the work done.
Since my leader has raised this question, I also wonder whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) paid 25 cents a page for his copy of the minutes. Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes a fundamental change and reform of our divorce law. The present grounds for divorce are a series of matrimonial offences. speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was waxing along last night about the minor attachment period.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: And you are waning today.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I hope to wane shortly. I was trying to bring to the minister's attention a problem in respect of the minor attachment period and the reason we should be thinking in terms of eliminating this period, making one attachment period which a claimant could understand without the assistance of a bureaucracy of lawyers, accountants and union officials.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Don't include lawyers.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
In any event, I think the minister misunderstood in that he thought I was seeking to reduce the minor attachment period to the existing attachment period. I am suggesting somewhere between the two, at a cost that would not be too significant in terms of the fund but would be worthy of looking at in terms of simplifying the whole program dealing with minor and major attachments to the working force.
This is an area that certainly should be investigated, because the eight-week attachment period and the time it

takes for one to re-establish his major attachment to the work force is a disincentive to re-employment. I do not think anyone, no matter where he stands in respect of the principle of unemployment insurance, is in favour of provisions which are in fact disincentives to those seeking employment from actually going out and looking for work.
I was dealing with matters I felt had not been canvassed in this legislation but that I think should be dealt with if we are going to clean up and improve the act. One of the difficulties for a long time-other members have mentioned this-is in relation to the question of entrapment by the operation of the benefit control system. There is no doubt that any claimant who has had explained to him carefully what he must do to qualify would never be disqualified, particularly if he knows the rules, because he would then know the kind of answers to give the benefit control officer. What has happened in the past is that those who have not had jobs, and were perhaps not as bright as some others, were being disqualified, while the sharpies were being allowed to continue to receive benefits. That is a system we do not want to see prevail.
What is needed is a whole new approach in respect of benefit control officers. I am talking about a human approach and not an approach by an RCMP officer attempting to get a confession from a criminal, which is much like what has happened in the past. The change would require a humanistic approach to the claimant, because the weak are now suffering and the strong are getting away. I think that no one in this House wants that situation to continue. We need clear legislative guidelines in respect of benefit control officers, and I think a careful look should be taken in respect of previous occupations.
In terms of the question of suitability of employment under this act we have not had any change. There are guidelines which are exercised when someone who is unemployed has a special skill. They do not have to drop the skill level immediately but are held at that level for a time. I am not sure of the formula, but as a result of discussions with certain individuals I understand that in fact the formula varies to some extent.
In any event, there is a formula, for example, whereby an unemployed teacher does not have to accept a job for a period of time if there is no teaching position available. This may apply also to an accountant, a welder or someone else. It is my view that where work is available, people should accept the work. I do not think we need an unemployment system which perpetuates a class system. I see no reason, if I should be unemployed, why I should not be required to take work that is available.
There is dignity involved in work: some of it may not be something a person would want to do for the rest of his or her life, but I do not think there is anything against moving up and down in the skilled levels when people are unemployed. I do not see why, after a period of time at a skilled level, they should not be required to take available work. In other words, I do not see why the chief chef of a hotel should not be required to flip hamburgers at Macdonald's if he is unemployed. I do not see anything wrong with that. I think the minister should pay attention to these points in respect of the amendments.
November 5, 1975

Too much attention has been paid by this House and the media to alleged abuses of the fund. The facts are clear: the cost to the fund as a result of abuses is minimal. I listened carefully last night to the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) who said that because of the deficit there must be something rotten in respect of the fund. The reason we have a deficit is clear: there is too much unemployment. There is nothing very complicated about that.
I defy the hon. member to cost the abuses and to tell me what percentage of the deficit is a direct result thereof. It is almost nil. I am not condoning this, because of course we should be as vigilant as we can in getting rid of any cheaters in view of the fact it destroys the fund and its credibility in the minds particularly of workers who are unhappy to pay for the cheaters. We in this party are just as unhappy as anybody else that there are abuses of the fund. The workers in the mill in my riding are not particularly happy to be paying for the guys the hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary suggests cheat. There is no reason why they should. So certainly we want to see enacted any kind of enforcement that will improve the operation of the fund.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary put forward some views which probably are widely believed, but I think there is a misconception in this regard. He started off by saying:
I think we must decide whether this should be a welfare scheme or an insurance scheme, Mr. Speaker. I submit it is really a welfare scheme. It has taught people not to work and, as a result, we are losing the work ethic in Canada.
That was the theme of his speech, yet he concluded with these words:
I received a telephone call today from one of my constituents who is approaching the age of 65. He has paid into the unemployment insurance plan all his life. Now that he is about to retire, he will not receive any benefit.
He cannot have it both ways. There happens to be a welfare provision within the fund. He wants to retain that but does not want to call it a welfare fund. There is a clear inconsistency here. In terms of the sort of philosophical approach the hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary takes, there has to be some welfare provision within the fund; it simply cannot be a bald fund dealing only with common aspects.
I should like to deal briefly with the amendments the minister is proposing. One of the more contentious is the question of the additional time one must wait when a quit occurs. Initially I was sympathetic to that view, and still am. In respect of those persons who quit, as opposed to those who are laid off as a result of lack of work, there should be a significant distinction in the length of time they wait before they are paid their cheque. Quite frankly, I think that if you have two people working on the same job and one is fired because of misconduct, or possibly because of a drinking or some other problem, and the other person is laid off because there is lack of work, it is inequitable that both should have approximately the same length of time to wait before they receive their benefits.
The difficulty in respect of such a provision is that a tremendous number of people are not legitimately fired for misconduct. There is great potential for abuse. There is
Unemployment Insurance Act
difficulty involved in extending the time for those who quit and thereby encouraging people to try to hold a job and at least to try to find another one while they are employed, rather than collect from the fund. I think this is a worth-while objective, but the difficulty is that no one has properly defined "misconduct", "just case" or the other qualification "refused suitable employment".
Even though there is a body of jurisprudence under the Unemployment Insurance Act, it is a vague generalization and there is still a bias in favour of the employer. In fact, the additional waiting period the minister seeks in the bill could work great hardship on some people. I have a tendency to favour the additional disqualification in the hope that we might have some tightening up, but I am not sure the minister is ready to tighten up the bias which naturally flows in favour of the employer. The reason for the bias in favour of the employer, first of all, is the attack by the media on the fund and the principle of unemployment insurance. This attack has been quite overwhelming. If one puts oneself in the position of either a benefit control officer, a board referee or even an umpire, one finds that the pressures by the press media and what one might see as the prevailing public climate create a tendency to see dishonesty where it does not exist, and a tendency to move against the person seeking the benefit because of the rumours heard about people skiing on Whistler Mountain wearing a "UIC Ski Bum" shirt. Therefore, there is a built-in bias in favour of the employer. So simply by extending the period of disqualification for benefits in respect of a quit, we do not cure the other half of the problem.
I submit the problem is that while there should be a distinction between those laid off and those who quit, we must take into account the other part, which is the question of defining fairly what is misconduct and what is just cause, and also correct the inbred bias in respect of the operation of the fund by the various officials within it. If that could be done, I would certainly support the principle the minister is attempting to place in the fund.
An incredible clause is the amendment to section 24(1) which deals with the reduction from 75 per cent of insurable earnings to 662/3 per cent. The minister has not attempted to make any distinction between those with dependants and those with none. I cannot imagine a more regressive step under the bill. I submit that the financial savings probably are not large. I do not have the figures and I do not know if it is the hard-heartedness of the minister or whether there is a real financial reason for the change, but considering that we are in an era when we have adopted, I think, a pretty firm philosophy that those with dependants should receive more benefits than those without-and the minister must surely have supported the family allowance provisions which this government instituted some time ago-it is difficult to understand why we take this regressive and retrograde step of denying dependants proper and adequate support under the unemployment insurance fund. It is clearly a conservative, retrogressive step.
If we continue to say that because we increased family allowances some years ago, therefore they do not need it- and that was the logic that allowed this government to

November 5, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
take away the milk and bread subsidies-we will wipe out all the social benefits that we have been successful in achieving over the past 15 or 20 years. You cannot keep saying: We have this program, therefore we will cut the other program. It is very clear that in this country the rich continue to get richer and the poor continue to get poorer, and every time this kind of legislation comes before the House it displays the kind of hard-heartedness that I did not really expect from this minister, although I might have expected it from some of his colleagues.
The other amendment with which I wanted to deal briefly concerns coverage to the age of 65. Without going into it in detail, the justification is the improvements that have occurred in terms of retirement benefits, and therefore this provision is unnecessary. If ever there is still a group in our society which needs the help of all of us, which needs continuing benefits, which needs additional health care, housing and all the other things we should be providing, it is those who are 65 and over-and to take away this benefit is a callous approach. The savings to the fund are minuscule and the benefits are significant to those who have spent their whole lives working. So I believe this to be an unfortunate move. The decision not to grant advance pay under section 28 is, again, clearly a retrogressive step. It is no skin off the government's nose to advance pay so someone does not have to get emergency food vouchers to keep himself going. Again, it is a hardhearted and callous approach to the act and certainly does not improve it in any way.
I think the coverage of LIP and LEAP sponsors is progressive. I think this is a mixed bag. There are amendments that certainly weaken the support. I think the changes in terms of maternity provisions are desirable, but of course the key problem in the bill and the key reason that I cannot support it is the change in the financial formula. If ever there was an abdication of the government's responsibility in terms of creating a society with full employment, here it is. To suggest that no longer do we rely on a 4 per cent unemployment rate, and to admit tacitly that in fact 7 per cent is a normal unemployment rate for this society, is a tragedy for Canada. It is a tragedy because before we know it, not only will governments but people will accept it; and that is where the permissive rot is starting.
We have heard a lot of talk here about the work ethic. I happen to be one who believes in it. I think we should do what we can to encourage the work ethic, but you do not encourage it when you have a government which says, "We will now think about 7 per cent as being a normal rate of unemployment rather than 4 per cent". You do not do it by having a government which does not give you unemployment projections when it is asked, and you do not do it by having a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who a year and a half ago said that maybe work is now becoming irrelevant and we are entering a new era, while shrugging his shoulders.
There is a certain consistency in that philosophy when you take that statement with the changes in the unemployment insurance fund and line up the two. That is where the abandonment of the work ethic is-it is on the government side. We are a party which believes in full employment. We believe in a guaranteed full employment act. We 
do not want unemployment. We have unemployment insurance because of the system we live under, but we still believe we can create a society where there is work for all. We want from each according to his ability, and to give to each according to his need.
When you say "from each according to his ability", that means everyone in our society has something to contribute to all of society. People tend to look at the NDP and say, "Oh well, you people are great as the welfare party. You have done fine on the social reform legislation and we recognize that". But they forget the second part of the socialist ethic which is absolutely key to our philosophy, and that is, from each according to his ability. This means full work for everyone, with everyone contributing and being a meaningful member of the society. It is that philosophy that has been abandoned, although I suppose it has never been accepted on the government side. That is why we oppose this legislation, because it still does not deal in any significant way with the question of unemployment.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am indeed much interested in taking part in the debate on this legislation, more especially as it gives me the opportunity to make the necessary clarifications regarding the problem of unemployment insurance in general.
Let me first of all point out the speech made in the House by my colleague the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne). I think he has demonstrated in a very thoughtful and specific way the real problems raised by this legislation. As he was telling me, we have here a series of efforts on the part of public servants with a view to improving the legislation. But unfortunately, those public servants seem to know nothing about the actual problems faced by unemployment insurance claimants. Indeed, it would seem that the problem of unemployment per se is not understood as it should be. While we would all tend to expect a definite improvement following the amendments brought in by the minister, we must unfortunately realize that this is only attempted improvement and that finally nothing has been improved with the introduction of those amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Apparently, this stems from the fact that there is hesitation about the very concept of unemployment, that is whether we should really help those who for any reason cannot remain in employment or whether the purpose of that Act is to help them, or still whether it is rather a fight to prevent the largest number possible of unemployed from receiving benefits.
Madam Speaker, when day in and day out one has to refer a tremendous number of cases submitted by unemployment insurance claimants, one does realize that it is often the second way of thinking which prevails, meaning that UIC officials are involved in a fight against the unemployed in order to prevent them from receiving benefits. Of course, this warps the fundamental principle enshrined in the Unemployment Insurance Act which is aimed at helping those in need since, even though they are unemployed, they must continue to live.
November 5, 1975

I understand that one should try to prevent any abuse from those who avail themselves of unemployment insurance benefits more or less honestly and even fraudulently. Of course, we understand this. There is no doubt that we would need to have a completely different system in order to eliminate the existing phenomenon of people seeking unemployment. Why does this phenomenon exist? It would take too long to go over all the explanations to show that it is caused by the deficiency of the system itself. We could partly solve this problem by accepting, for instance, to implement in Canada, an annual guaranteed minimum income plan such as that favored by the Social Credit Party, but since we have not reached that point yet and since the government seems determined not to accept any such proposal, we can only criticize, as objectively as possible, the minister's proposals concerning improvements to the existing Unemployment Insurance Act.
I therefore say that under this policy of trying to prevent people from receiving unemployment insurance when they do not necessarily have the right to do so, we are being utterly unfair towards those who really need and are truly entitled to benefits. Bill C-69 contains nothing which could completely eliminate the problems that stems from the present legislation, and we deplore it. On the contrary, the government seems to add even further problems. For instance, it was already difficult enough for people aged 65 to support all the pressures placed on them to prevent them from being truly unemployed when they were dealing with the unemployment insurance office. The government think they can solve the problem by saying: Well, people aged 65 or over will no longer be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Madam Speaker, others have said so before me, but I would like to repeat that this is an outrageous case of discrimination.
And until it is proven that the individual who is 65 can no longer work it is discriminatory to suggest that at 65 someone is ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits, and I think in addition that is a direct attack against the work of those people most of whom are now 65 and plain manual workers. Most of them started to work at the age of 15 which means that quite often they have been working for 50 years. So they paid unemployment insurance since the legislation came into effect. They cannot get it in their heads, no matter the explanations that could be given to them, that they are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits if they are still capable of working, even though they may be on compulsory retirement.
So we are against this amendment which reduces the possibility of benefits from 70 to 65.
Another aspect of the bill seems to spell improvement, but it is so shy that it cannot be termed real improvement. It is the extension apparently granted to those who leave their job because of illness. We should have made here a much clearer, a much more precise improvement as, once more, it is already distressing enough to have to leave a job because of employment shortage or because you become physically unable to work and we should not worsen the situation of a person unable to work because of illness. It is already distressing enough to be ill and it should not be worsened by all kinds of petty annoyances concerning the initial period or the additional period. Madam Speaker, this is certainly a reason that should be readily accepted at
Unemployment Insurance Act
the same level as regular unemployment insurance because any man obviously needs an income to live and when he is sick it is even worse and even more distressing. This is why I expected the minister to accept sickness as a valid motive-just as employment shortage is-and also to make it easier for pregnant women to draw unemployment insurance benefits. It would be a good way to recognize the contribution of women at a time when they encourage population growth in Canada.
Madam Speaker, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, when we see that this bill tries without any results to improve the legislation and that we can feel an underlying desire to further restrict those who claim unemployment insurance benefits, we must conclude that this bill is not satisfying and does not meet the actual interests of the people. And in a period like the present one where an unemployment problem really exists, it is not the right time to complicate the situation even more. And I repeat, the unemployed has to live.
Madam Speaker, if we really wished to improve the unemployment insurance legislation we should change its principle. It should rather become employment insurance. If we had a commission deeply committed to find employment, and possibly create some so that a person would not have to be left without income by reason of shortage, then it would be another matter. But in spite of all the suggestions made, instead of paying unemployment insurance benefits, it would now be possible to promote local initiative projects for instance. We could even transfer part of the moneys paid the unemployment insurance fund to local initiative projects, because it is always more meaningful to pay people for providing a service, for producing something. But not only does it appear that the amounts allocated to those projects will not be increased but, in keeping with the last guidelines set forth by the Prime Minister himself, even those expenses are to be cut down.
In that case, I would urge the minister to make up for the lack of employment-and therefore the necessity of paying benefits to a far greater number of unemployed- by simply providing incentives for job creation, one of which might be local initiatives. This would be a first step towards employment insurance instead of unemployment insurance as we now experience.
Madam Speaker, in concluding my short remarks, I would stress the fact that whatever the situation in our country now, a legislation should never punish those who have no option but to apply for unemployment insurance benefits. In other words, I would even say interpretations of the act should be more in favour of claimants rather than systematically aim at opposing them. For one, two or three unemployed workers who might appear to have a stretchable conscience when it comes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, there may be one who will be punished although he has an absolute right to benefits. Even if it were only to avoid unfair treatment for that claimant, I think the act should always be interpreted in its widest meaning. I make this recommendation for I am sure that all my colleagues here in this House also have had many times to deal with unemployment problems submitted to them by their constituents.
We are well aware of all the difficulties experienced by some claimants. Now that we try to improve the legislation

November 5, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
on unemployment insurance, we should be careful and try to give those who unfortunately rely on such panacea the possibility of enjoying a decent life with unemployment insurance benefits. We should not force people to struggle constantly against the legislation and the civil servants. We should rather take the first alternative, namely to really help the taxpayer.
Madam Speaker, unfortunately I do not expect this bill to bring any necessary improvements and I hope that the committee will propose serious amendments to this act so that the Unemployment Insurance Commission be really upgraded.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the amendments proposed by the minister are the result of a post mortem conducted after the 1972 election by the then nearly-defeated Liberal government. That took its toll and a minister was removed from responsibility at that time. I think they realized that the amendments they originally proposed and the hand-outs they thought the public was going to accept so gratefully were working against their interests as a political party. It took them several years to bring in the amendments. All the comments made during the election of 1972 have not stopped since, with constituents reminding members of parliament that something should be done to introduce amendments in the House of Commons to rectify things.
The public did not accept what it was told when the 1971 amendments were introduced, and it has not accepted it since. The public was looking for restraint at that time, and it is looking for it today. Unfortunately, the measures proposed by the minister will not bring about the changes the public wants and which it has pointed to on so many occasions. We have to bear in mind what the public has said and what it will say about these changes that have been introduced.
Unless the minister is prepared to accept some changes, the proposals he has made will not go far enough. They do not deal squarely with the problems. We are faced with the prospect of a $4 billion bill, whether it is paid by the federal government, the employer or the employee. That is a frightening amount. We often wonder what has brought about inflation. I think the public is aware that it is the measures we have introduced in this House. We do not restrain ourselves in many instances. Many of the measures introduced were simply vote-getters for the Liberals in 1972. The public is aware of the cost and it has had its share of socialism.
For years the New Democratic Party has been saying that what this country needs is socialism, but now we realize what socialism has done. It has brought us to our knees and given us the most stringent restrictions on labour and management to the point where they are feuding. We are told to tighten our belts, but the public has been telling us for years to tighten the unemployment insurance belt. It is not that they wish to deprive people who require it, because the public can be fair, but people are aware of what is going on in the community and in many instances know who is drawing unemployment insurance.

But what is the point of singling out one individual and cutting him or her off benefits? What the people want is a clean sweep of the entire unemployment insurance scheme. It does not do an employee who has been contributing for years any good to see a fellow worker collecting benefits and living on his back. The person who has been working and contributing thinks he might as well have the money as see it go down the drain. This is an attitude of many people.
It is time we faced reality, Madam Speaker. Canadians should be told how much individuals have been drawing in welfare benefits. It is not unemployment insurance any more; it is unemployment welfare. This is what the government intended by introducing these measures. The minister says that because you draw old age security at age 55 you cannot have another form of welfare. That is an admission that it has become a welfare scheme. The public does not want that; what it expects is an honest proposal. The public agrees to insurance against unemployment, but not to a welfare scheme.
If you drive a car and have a series of accidents, your insurance premiums are raised. If there are repeated fires in your factory, clearly there is something wrong with your management and sometimes you will be refused fire insurance. Why should it be any different with unemployment? The present program encourages people to draw unemployment insurance. Why not reward people who reach age 65 without drawing unemployment insurance. I say that if you have not drawn unemployment insurance, you should be rewarded. That would give one an incentive to work. Or if a man has been unlucky enough to be fired, laid off-even if he quits-the prospect of reward would encourage him to look for work. We could incorporate several weeks of forgiveness so that if a man is without work for a short period it will not be held against him. Certainly, if a man has not drawn money from the scheme he should be rewarded. Let us be consistent. Why should the steady worker's contribution be as large as that proposed?
We should take stock. Certainly, if an individual has constantly drawn on the fund, something is wrong. Perhaps he is in the wrong job. Perhaps his seasonal work leads to seasonal unemployment. Perhaps something is the matter with the individual himself. Perhaps that individual should be encouraged to look for a job in another area and get out of a rut. Sometimes a man knows what will happen year in and year out. That should be changed. The program should provide incentive for a man to look for work. Unfortunately, the present bill does nothing of the kind.
As I have said, we should reward those who work steadily. I am not suggesting any hard and fast rule. Surely the officials of the department can examine this idea. For instance, if someone has contributed steadily for 10, 15 or 20 years and has not drawn on the fund, he should be encouraged not to quit his job. We hear of people who are encouraged to keep their jobs after they are 65. Why should every employee quit at 65? I know what the regulations will say about the age of claimants, but I suggest you can circumvent regulations of that kind.
November 5, 1975

I say that we should once more make this an insurance scheme. The public would be grateful if the government once more were to make the unemployment insurance scheme a true insurance scheme. People do not like the present welfare scheme. In smaller communities of the kind which I and others in this House represent you could advertise jobs in the local post office. There is no point in going to the local Manpower office for workers. I have tried, and IV2 years after my inquiry help has been offered. Often the employers in small communities are looking for workers, but the local Manpower offices do not know about these workers.
I say it is a waste of time applying at local Manpower offices. Frankly, I do not know why people bother asking the offices for help. Why not put up on a notice board at the local post office the list of those persons drawing unemployment insurance, together with their qualifications? Then an employer who wants a worker can go to the post office and see what kind of help is available. This would be a simple procedure. In rural areas particularly, employers might want to hire workers on a short-time basis. At least those workers would be off the welfare rolls.
Perhaps we could provide a lump sum payment as a reward to those who have not drawn unemployment insurance over the years. I agree that some cannot carry on without resorting to unemployment insurance. Why not set up an unemployment insurance loan fund from which the unemployed could borrow and avoid the stigma of being an unemployment insurance recipient? They could borrow from the fund to tide them over until the next job. There could be a payback scheme. We could use many methods.
The trouble is that the minister and the department will not listen when we say the program should be an insurance scheme and not a welfare scheme. The government says that we cannot manage without unemployment insurance, that we have on our hands a revolution of sorts, that the people are rebellious and to stop complaints we must provide them with huge unemployment insurance payments. Somebody must pay-that is my complaint-and the people doing the paying are not those doing the drawing. I know that many would not complain aloud, even if so inclined. They think: I am helping somebody else. But since the government is asking the public to restrain its wage demands, I say it must cut spending somewhere.
The present bill merely increases a tax. The government is doing this for its own political benefit. It is up to the government to relieve the pressure on the taxpayer, to relieve the pressure on those who work hard and owe everything to the honest sweat of their brow. The government must show leadership. Instead of asking the House of Commons to increase both the employer and employee contributions, the government should consider ways to reduce contributions and save some of this money. Why does it distinguish between employer and employee contributions? Apparently, when government supporters mention employers they automatically think of huge employers who own factories, hide assets and rig books. Apparently, if you are an employer you are rich automatically. The minister appears to single out employers. Why add to their burdens? I cannot understand why the small employer who is willing to hire a few workers should pay a premium 1.4 times greater than that paid by the employee.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Why the discrimination? After all, the employer is doing his share by employing that individual. He had to keep the books. Try to submit a late deduction and you are penalized. This was a political gimmick, nothing more, to make it appear that the government is on the side of labour. Who is the employer? In many instances, a simple businessman who himself is struggling for survival. If he closes down his shop, both he and his employee are without a job. I employ people on a little farm I operate. My worker has Saturday or Sunday off and I have to sit there on a Sunday afternoon while the sun is shining, keeping the books and making sure everything is figured out. If I do not, someone in the department will send me a nice letter threatening me with a penalty. Small businessmen have appealed to me from time to time to get this aspect cleared up if ever an opportunity presented itself.
I suppose there are cases of individuals taking advantage of the scheme. On the other hand, there are plenty of individuals who do not draw benefits to which they are entitled. I have received complaints from people who honestly answered the questions directed to them, but the commission comes along with trick questions designed not to get information but to fix things up so that claims need not be paid. I am all for action being taken in cases where there is an attempt to deceive, but I want the commission to be honest when it comes to the type of questions asked. After all, if a person has been getting $4 an hour and he is asked what he expects to receive, he is going to say $4 an hour; he does not tell the commission he expects to receive $2 an hour. If they asked whether he would be prepared to work for less, the answer might be different. Instead, they say afterwards that the applicant is restricting himself because nobody is prepared to pay $4 an hour in his area.
It is often difficult to get employment in rural areas because there are so few employers. The commission seeks to avoid payment of claims by telling applicants that they are restricting themselves because they want to work in their own areas. But, Madam Speaker, that is where their families are living. I know cases where the commission tried to send applicants from Saskatchewan to look for work in the heart of Ontario, leaving their families with no certainty they would find permanent employment. It was just a way of disentitling the claimant, and this is not what the insurance scheme was set up to do. It was not set up to make things difficult; it was put there to help in time of need.
A great many applicants, especially those who for various reasons lack sufficient education, do not know where these comparatively simple questions are leading. They give the answers which they think are correct, and then, bingo, there is confusion for three or four weeks, after which a demand is made for repayment of benefits. No doubt it occurred to someone that it would look good to check over a few of the claims. I am sure no member wants that kind of complaint to be referred to him. It is true that upon reviewing the situation the commission often agrees to reconsider the decision, but I say we should not find ourselves in such a situation.
First, we should provide an incentive not to use the fund except in cases of real emergency. This might be done through requiring a lower premium in certain circum-

November 5, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
stances. Or it might be possible to make limited sums available as loans in appropriate cases to bridge temporary unemployment. Then, again, an arrangement might be made for workers to receive a credit from the fund on their retirement in acknowledgment of the fact that they had never become a burden to society. Such a plan might lead to a net benefit since, as things are, there are many who say to themselves, "If I am going to pay for the rest of my life and get nothing, I had better find a way of getting some of the money back before I retire." Such an attitude might well be the result of the amendments in the bill before us concerning workers who reach the age of 65.
I express the hope that the minister will be receptive to these ideas. I have known a lot of politicians in my day and many of them find it difficult to talk about unemployment insurance because, of course, there are voters back home who will be paying attention. Also, there is always another political party ready to accuse them of being against the interests of the workers.
I say to the minister that every worker wants amendments which are sensible and fair. They want the government to show restraint. Above all, they want guidance from the minister. Hopefully, the hon. gentleman can find time to consider the suggestions which have been made to him, and I hope that in committee some of the complaints which have been conveyed to us and expressed in this House will be taken seriously. I trust he will not view any concession he may make as an expression of surrender to another political party. We in this party have put forward our ideas in such a way that their adoption may even be helpful to him politically, and if that is the case, fine.
We want to see the fund back into such a good position that there will no longer be any question of increasing the premiums to be paid either by the employees, the employers or the federal government. Instead, we want the fund and the economy to be placed on such a firm footing that the hon. gentleman is able to say; "We are reducing the premiums because we have got the problem licked."

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thus far about the only agreement reached in this debate is that the Unemployment Insurance Act is a mess. Where the difficulty arises is over the question whether it is an insurance scheme or a welfare scheme. This is an important question because the issue of an increase in premiums really hinges upon the answer. Then one must ask oneself another question: Who is responsible for unemployment? Is it the government, or is it society collectively as represented by the government? If it is an insurance scheme, then obviously it is right to raise premiums. If it is a welfare scheme, not only should premiums not be raised but premiums should be abandoned altogether. If unemployment is the responsibility of the government it makes no sense to suggest that premiums should be raised. If unemployment is something that you cannot do anything about, then it is a social problem that must be borne by society in general.
Let me make my own position quite clear, Madam Speaker. It seems to me that the Unemployment Insurance Act has in fact become a welfare scheme. Since unemployment is a social problem, it should be the responsibility of

the government. In either case, those responsibilities are not individual responsibilities but social responsibilities and as such should be borne out of some form of general taxation rather than financed by premiums. This is the argument I wish to make.
It seems to me that we are going absolutely in the wrong direction. The government is trying to shuffle off its responsibility in both these areas by putting the load on the individual instead of accepting responsibility both for the rate of unemployment and the fact that unemployment insurance is a cross-subsidization scheme. It is true that when unemployment insurance was first introduced into this country it was a reasonable insurance program, but over the years governments in Canada have moved it from an insurance program to a welfare program. They have brought various people into the scheme. There may have been good reasons for doing this, but nevertheless by bringing in groups like fishermen, seasonal workers and farm labourers, the government has destroyed any credibility that the scheme had for being called an insurance scheme.
An insurance plan depends on unpredictability. That is what insurance is all about, whether it be car insurance or fire insurance. It depends upon not knowing who is going to have an accident or a fire, and under what circumstances. Fishermen have been brought into the scheme, and we know fishermen will be unemployed every year for a certain number of months. We also know that farm labourers of certain kinds will be unemployed. These events are predictable. This is why it is not an insurance scheme but a subsidy program.
As I say, if it is a subsidy or welfare program-and a good argument can probably be made for having a subsidy or welfare program in this area-then it should be accepted as a total social responsibility instead of calling it an insurance scheme. Whatever credibility the plan may have had initially for being called an insurance program has been destroyed by government after government. I think we must recognize the scheme for what it is.
There is nothing wrong with calling it a welfare program, but if it is a welfare program let us treat it as such and not perpetuate the fraud of calling it an insurance scheme, asking people to pay a premium and telling them that the premium is somehow related to the risk involved. It is a cross-subsidization program, which means that one province is subsidizing another province, that one industry is subsidizing another industry, that one group of workers is subsidizing another group of workers. In the social context there is nothing wrong with that; this is done through redistribution programs of various kinds. But that is not insurance and it does not call for premium payments but for the application of a general taxation policy.
Since government either cannot or will not do anything about unemployment, it must assume responsibility for funding this scheme instead of throwing this burden on the shoulders of the individual. In proposing amendments to increase premiums, the government is saying, "We cannot do anything very much about unemployment but we are going to make you pay for it. We are going to make you pay for the failure of government policy and planning. We will take ourselves off the hook and make you pay for it". That is grossly unfair. No government is entitled to
November 5, 1975

absolve itself from that kind of responsibility at the expense of the individual workers of this country.
Everyone rattles the Unemployment Insurance Act, yet everyone is guilty of abusing it. I do not think you could point the finger at any one group of our society or at any one province; everyone is guilty. I have listened with considerable interest to my hon. friends in the Conservative party denouncing the Unemployment Insurance Act. Yet whenever I ask them what they would do, I do not hear very many constructive proposals. They do not tell me which groups they would remove from the plan. In criticizing the Unemployment Insurance Act, denouncing its inequities and telling horror stories about the act, in saying that the act is not generous enough to certain groups, not one member has made a speech critical of the Unemployment Insurance Act without saying, "I know all kinds of cases of individual injustice". But hon. members cannot talk out of both sides of their mouths. They almost won the 1972 election by their attacks on the Unemployment Insurance Act, yet at no time did I hear any constructive proposals for improving the act.
The truth of the matter is that very few of us can be totally critical of the Unemployment Insurance Act for fear of offending our constituents. Of all the political parties in this House, the Conservatives have the most fear of offending their constituents because so many of them are living off unemployment insurance.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I am being a little rough, Madam Speaker, but I am being rough intentionally. I get fed up with the cant on this whole subject. Everyone is for motherhood, truth and justice until it comes to doing something to improve matters. They say $4 billion is too much to spend. But which groups would they eliminate from the plan? Would they eliminate farm labourers, fishermen, loggers, or maternity benefits? Where would they make cuts? I have yet to hear their program on that.
It reminds me of the sort of arguments made during the election campaign about cutting government expenditure. The only cut that they suggested really was Information Canada. When they were asked what government expenditure they would cut, whether they would get rid of old age pensions, or family allowances, they would not answer. The same can be said of all these critics of the Unemployment Insurance Act. When you ask these people what benefits they would remove, they do not reply. They do not reply because they are afraid of their own constituents. They are afraid of offending them. They try to please both sides-those who do not like the plan and those who live off it. That is the great dilemma we are facing. We have created a Frankenstein for ourselves. We cannot live with it yet we cannot live without it.
The present system of premiums should be abolished and replaced by a general tax, perhaps not by an income tax because that is high enough already, but some kind of payroll tax. This would make more sense than employer and employee paying individual premiums. For example, we might use a system similar to workmen's compensation. In that event, if we wanted an insurance scheme we could risk-relate it to the industry involved. Every industry has a pattern. The way in which workmen's compensation is
Unemployment Insurance Act
risk-related has had a marked effect on the attitude of industry toward safety. When their premium goes up they do something about safety in their plant. Not as much as they should, but there is some improvement. It seems to me we should do the same thing with unemployment insurance.
Many industries in this country could not survive without the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The biggest abusers, while having the loudest mouths, are the inefficient industries of this country that live off the Unemployment Insurance Act and do more to abuse the act than any individual in our society. For example, the fruit growers have criticized the act and said how much they suffer under it, how terrible it is for them. I came back to Ottawa on a plane one day with a gentleman from the Okanagan Valley who ran a fruit farm. He was very critical of the Unemployment Insurance Act and then went on to tell me how he hired married women for eight weeks and promised them at least eight weeks' work so they could qualify for unemployment insurance and he could pay them the minimum wage. He could not run his farm without the Unemployment Insurance Act. He depends on unemployment insurance in order to get his labourers, and he is not the only one; there are all kinds of industries like that in our society.
This system is very convenient for them. They take on labourers like a commodity and they let them go like a commodity, at which time the labourers go back on unemployment insurance and society pays for it. If they did not have this scheme to fall back on, these people might be a little more responsible in the way they treat their employees. They would have to be a little more efficient in the way they run their industries; they could not run them from the seat of their pants, hiring and firing at will.
Let me give an interesting illustration of that in respect of the automobile industry. There was a time when that industry had extensive lay-offs in good years and in bad years. They always said that the models changed, so that everyone had to be laid off for six weeks or two months. This was the case until the unions said that if the industry continued to lay them off in this way, they would have to pay the employees during those lay-offs. They brought in an agreement under which, if the employees were laid off, the companies had to pay them.
The automobile industry suddenly found that the work was not as seasonal as they once thought it to be. They began to keep everyone on all year long. They evened out their level of production, instead of hiring thousands of employees and working the hell out of them for part of the time and laying them off for two months. They levelled out the work in the industry. This has been the case, generally speaking, for the last five or six years since the unions negotiated that kind of agreement. There has been steady employment, as there should be, in the automobile industry since then. But at one time they dragged in thousands of people when they were required and laid them off when they were not, giving the industry this yo-yo effect.
Unemployment insurance permits this kind of thing to take place. It is important to note that in this kind of society which is disorganized and free-wheeling, a back-

November 5, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
ward society, we have no alternative to unemployment insurance; we could not exist without unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance is required by this Liberal government which cannot manage its affairs, cannot provide full employment and has no plan for the economy. The government uses this means of preventing a revolution taking place. If the government did not have that kind of support, the people would not be able to live in this kind of society.
People have many needs, whether they be housing, transportation or other things which are required. There are many needs in the world today. How can there be unemployment with this system that treats labour as a commodity? This liberal society does not have an answer, so the government brings in unemployment insurance. It is much like LIP, which is a sort of middle-class welfare scheme. This government cannot solve the problems, so it pays the people off. Unfortunately, it is not the government that foots the bill for this type of welfare scheme. The individuals who pay are those who are industrious and work. Those are the individuals who pay for this scheme. Those are the individuals this government wants to pay even more.
In some ways, unemployment insurance would not bother me. It would not be of great concern to me whether unemployment insurance were an insurance scheme or a welfare plan, if in fact it helped the poor. If the people needed help so badly, I would not quarrel about how they got that help. The problem with this unemployment insurance scheme is that, generally speaking, the money does not go to the poor. All of us know from experience in our ridings that the poor are the first ones to be knocked off benefits. They are not clever enough, in most cases, to know how to work the Unemployment Insurance Act. The ones who know how to and do work the Unemployment Insurance Act are the middle-class people.
There was an interesting story that appeared in the Globe and Mail on April 4 this year, from which I should like to quote. It appeared at page 7 and reads as follows:
In the 1973 figures, $686,000 in unemployment insurance went to Canadians with declared incomes of $25,000 a year and above; $20,000 of that going to persons with incomes in excess of $50,000 a year.
This is the fine scheme we have in this country! Of course, if you ask anyone about this they are likely to tell you the scheme should not differentiate in this way. That is how badly this whole thing is screwed up. We all know that the people who benefit most from unemployment insurance are seasonal workers who make more in a short season than many people who work all year long. West coast fishermen work four months a year and earn an average of $20,000. They then collect unemployment insurance for the rest of the time. What they do with that time, I do not know. Fishing in this country, with few exceptions, is not an occupation but a hobby. We are paying those people for engaging in that hobby.
I could give other examples of that where people around the country are engaged in fun activities. I once had a fellow from Newfoundland in my riding. He worked at a job but got into a few little brawls in the shop. If he did not like the foreman, he felt that he should punch him on the nose. After all, he is a bad guy and one should hit him.

There are many people who are not very understanding about these things, and he lost his job.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Like the guy who gets it on the nose.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That fellow lost his job and found it very difficult to understand. He had said some terrible things and hit the foreman, but had then forgiven him. He could not understand what the trouble was and why he should have lost his job. He looked for another job but found it very difficult to find one. After some difficulty, I thought we had him all calmed down and he found another job. I heard afterwards that he was doing very well and was to be made a foreman. This kid was only 22 years of age and had it made.
I thought we had accomplished something, and I suppose society would think he had been ground down into the dust and would conform. Then one day when I was on the train coming back to Ottawa I met this young lad and asked him where he was going. He said he was going home. I said, "Are you going home to visit your parents?" He said, "No; I am going home to stay. I have quit the job". I said, "I thought you were doing very well". He said, "Mr. Saltsman, that is not the way to live, getting up every morning at six o'clock, going to work, punching the time-clock. When the fishing season is here, they want you to work; when the hunting season is here, they want you to go to work."
He said, "They want you to work all year round. I am going home to do some fishing. When the fishing is not good, I will go on unemployment insurance. That's the way to live, Mr. Saltsman". You know, I think he is right. If your have a choice between living as a free soul or being chained to a machine, you should live as a free soul. Not everyone has that choice.
That is an exaggeration in order to make a point. However, the truth of the matter is that the people who pay for everything in this society are those who get up at six o'clock in the morning, whether it is raining, cold or hot, and go to work day after day, week after week, month after month. They do not have the opportunity to opt out. They usually are not unemployed and are not looking around for meaningful work. They do not say they want to stretch their horizons, but they pay for everything. They pay for unemployment insurance and they pay the taxes in this country-and they have no way out. This is the man the government is now saying must pay even more than he has paid, because the government cannot handle the problems of this society. There is great difficulty in discussing unemployment insurance because so little is known about the workings of the act and about who benefits and who pays. As I am saying this, I look across at the minister and see that he is there with a knowing smile on his face as if he knows. If he does know, he is not telling us. I sometimes suspect that the government does know all about cross-subsidization. I suspect it

knows who is bearing the cost of unemployment insurance and who is getting the benefits. This suits the purposes of the government and it suits its purpose not to discuss it or talk about it because too many horror stories may come out.
My quarrel is not about unemployment insurance, which I think is a very necessary and important program in the society in which we live; my quarrel arises because this program has been so distorted and twisted that it is now an open invitation to cheat. I know of very few cases where individuals have really defrauded the Unemployment Insurance Act in the sense that they have done something dishonest or something they were not allowed to do under the act.
What happens is that frequently people spend a great deal of time examining the loopholes in the act and figuring out ways to circumvent having to work and still be paid, rather than search for work. That is a serious problem in our society. It is not so bad in our society that we think chaos will ensue tomorrow. That is not so; there is still a strong work ethic in society. What happens, however, is that the man who works hard, who feels he has a responsibility to work, and who rather than accept benefits really tries hard, becomes very downhearted. It is not only that those who take advantage do so, but many of them make a point of going back to the job and telling him he is a fool to work. They usually exaggerate the situation. Then the steady workers feel like fools for working and sometimes ask themselves why they should continue to work. That is a serious problem for society.
Although unemployment insurance is costing our society $4 billion, it seems to me it is a good thing that money is being spent, whether or not it is being spent fairly. I hate to think of the state our society would be in now if that purchasing power were not being pumped back into society.
While I do not like the operation of the act, I will not quarrel with it at this time for the reasons I have given. We will not always be in a state of unemployment. We will have to get out of it some time. It is important to devise an act that appears to be fair to the people who must pay for the benefits. We must do that because society is held together when people are willing to work and share some of the rewards of that work with others. If they are not willing to share, then it does not matter whether we are talking about a capitalist society or a socialist society, because any society is based on the willingness of people to work and if that willingness is denied we are in serious trouble.
I suggest that the Unemployment Insurance Act does exactly that and is badly in need of change and correction. In some ways the act should be liberalized. I do not see any reason for there being a qualifying period of eight weeks or 20 weeks. If a person is willing to work, and if the job is not too restrictive, he should be entitled to collect unemployment insurance if society does not provide a job for him. There is no justification at all for the eight-week qualifying period. Most of these eight-week periods are phony, in any event. They are manufactured. I think of pregnancy and sickness claims, although I do not know
Unemployment Insurance Act how one could call pregnancy a sickness or an accident. I suppose in some cases it could be an accident. Generally speaking, it should not be either. What is the justification for saying a woman who puts in a 20-hour week in a shop, which may be the only 20-hour week she has put in in her life working in a shop, is entitled to a pay-out, while another woman who remains at home with a sick child is not entitled to anything?
If we come to the conclusion that this kind of payment should be made, surely every woman with a child is entitled to it, rather than just someone who can manoeuvre the Unemployment Insurance Act. There is no justification for this. At some point the minister will have to make up his mind concerning what he really wants. One day, depending on how the wind blows, he states that he will close all the loopholes in the act, and another day he makes statements such as the one I am about to quote. I refer to a statement he made before the Senate Committee on National Finance, on June 18, 1975. He said:
I must reaffirm that workers will not be forced to accept jobs that they do not want.
I presume he would also say, "or stay on jobs they do not want". Yet he will take the three-week disqualification period and change it to six weeks. What sense does that make? If the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act is to give people a greater opportunity to prove that they want to work, then obviously it makes no sense to increase or decrease the qualification period. That is not where the problem lies. Someone who wishes to quit a job does not go to the foreman and hit him. He finds a better way of getting fired.
Most employers are very guilty in the sense that they will seldom put down the real reason for a person leaving employment, because they want that person back. Very often these lay-offs take place in collusion with the employer. Most people who leave jobs would not be collecting unemployment insurance at all if the employer did not collude with them. Yet the employer is not investigated to the same extent as the employee.
I feel strongly about this bill in the sense that, despite everything the minister has said and despite all the trumpeting about the great changes taking place, we will not see the unemployment insurance pay-off come down a cent, despite these extra disqualification periods, because this is not where the problem really is: the problem is with the entire philosophy and approach to the act. This government is not prepared to bring in changes to manage the economy in the way in which it should be managed.
So long as that situation exists, we will always have abuses in respect of the Unemployment Insurance Act, because businessmen who harp about the abuses in respect of the Act will always look to themselves before looking to anyone else-they are the great abusers of the act, and those who support this system make such an unemployment insurance act necessary.
