Mr. Speaker, I believe the House is anxious to get to a vote on the second reading of this bill this afternoon. Therefore, I shall make my remarks at this point briefer than otherwise would have been the case. I want to make as clear as I can and in the simplest way possible that we will vote against
8894

November 5, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
this bill because it imposes additional burdens on the little people in this country. It is just as simple as that.
The minister and his colleagues can point to some improvements in Bill C-69 over the Unemployment Insurance Act as it now stands, but the effect of its major proposals is to place more of the burden of unemployment insurance on the little people and to add to the abuses which the little and ordinary people will suffer.
I want to say we in this party are glad we have unemployment insurance as part of our social structure. We are glad the trade union movement in the early years of this century campaigned for an unemployment insurance program such as already existed in other industrial and democratic countries. I will even say I welcome the fact that in 1919 the Liberal party at its great convention of that year pledged itself to bring in unemployment insurance along with old age pensions and health insurance.
I was proud of the fact that in 1925 and 1926 my predecessor, the late J. S. Woodsworth, in a minority parliament used his strength to put pressure on the government of that day in this field. In the main he tried to get both unemployment insurance and old age pensions. He got old age pensions from Mr. King, but so far as unemployment insurance was concerned, he only got a promise that that would come in later. Well, it finally came before parliament in 1940 and into effect in 1941.
I join the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) in saying that our economy today, apart from the fact that there would be great suffering on the part of individuals, would be in a great deal worse condition than it is if it were not for unemployment insurance. Therefore, we are supporters of the whole idea of unemployment insurance and we want to see it continued as part of our economic and social structure. But we want it to be a scheme that is fair. We want the burden of unemployment, which is a social responsibility, to be borne by society as a whole, not just by those who suffer most from unemployment or the fear of unemployment. We want the cost to be distributed on a basis that is fair. That is not the case at the present time and, what is even worse, this bill will take us still further in the direction of unfairness.
Let me list four or five ways in which, in our view, the bill does what I have said it does, that is, puts heavier burdens on the little people, and for these reasons we shall vote no on the motion for second reading. First, may I refer to the fact that the bill does nothing to resolve the abuses that are perpetrated on claimants. There has been a good deal of talk in this debate about abuse, although most of it has been the other way, but from all sides of the House there have been examples of abuse that individuals suffer, mainly because of the activities of benefit control officers, mainly because of the fact that there is no satisfactory definition of suitable employment. The provision cutting off thousands of claimants from benefits altogether or of cutting them back substantially because they are restricting their availability is not in keeping with the purpose and the principles of unemployment insurance. That is something that is not in this amending bill and it is one of the reasons we are opposed to it.

Another way in which this bill is hard on little people, and this has been put forward by my colleagues and by members in other parties, is the decision to reduce from 75 per cent to 66% per cent the amount of benefit available to those who are in special need and who have dependants. No matter what kind of case the minister might try to make for treating all alike, he cannot get around the fact that that is increasing the burden that is placed on little people, and that is what is wrong with this measure.
Another thing that is wrong with it is the proposal to double the period of disqualification to which certain claimants can be subjected from a maximum of three weeks to a maximum of six weeks on top of the waiting period. This will simply add to the economic difficulties, the deprivation and suffering of many of our people. Who are the people who will suffer because of this? It may include some of the people who have been talked about here who abuse the system, but the tragedy is that it will include a great many honest people who have rights under this act but will have those rights curtailed by this provision.
Then there is the provision about the level at which the government picks up the cost. This, of course, is a matter that has been referred to by many hon. members because it is one of the main provisions of the bill. At the present time, as everyone knows, the premiums going into unemployment insurance are expected to pay the total cost of its benefits so long as unemployment does not exceed 4 per cent. Above that point, the government is supposed to pick up the tab, which in fact it does.
This means that at present the cost of unemployment insurance is borne partly on the basis of a regressive form of taxation on all people at a firm percentage, despite the fact that they are the little people, but part of it, the cost of unemployment over 4 per cent, comes out of general revenue which, to a more reasonable extent, is achieved through the practice of the principle of the ability to pay. But the new proposal is that that threshold is to be raised so that it will be a sliding average of the actual unemployment in the country over the immediately preceding eight-year period. This means that in the years that lie ahead, the threshold at which the government will come in will get closer and closer to the actual level of unemployment in that year. In other words, the cost of unemployment insurance is being put more and more on the shoulders of those who are actually working, those in low-income and middle-income brackets.
This is a departure still furtner from the principle of paying for social benefits according to ability to pay. The government does this in so many ways. We have it in our income tax structure, we have it in Bill C-73, we have it across the board. It is a constant battle to try to get our society to recognize the principle of the ability to pay, and we are sorry to see this minister go in the other direction in this piece of legislation.
The other item I wish to mention again-one that has been mentioned several times, but I am simply putting them all together in one package-is an illustration of the additional burden being put on the little people in the decision to cut people off from either contributing to or drawing from unemployment insurance after the age of 65. I regard as most specious the argument that we have heard
November 5, 1975

from the minister-a good many Liberals have trotted it out as well-that the rationale for this is that the government is now doing very well for our older people. We have had the list of things that are available, such as old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan, and so on.
Whenever we talk about the fact that there are no opportunities in these programs to enable people to keep up with the rising cost and rising standard of living, when we insist on substantial increases in these pensions, we are told from the other side that all these benefits are indexed, that they are escalated either quarterly or annually. That is a snare and a delusion if I have ever heard one. Ordinarily, in society the workers in trade union groups who are seeking collective agreements and those who are unorganized. do not seek just a COLA arrangement, just an increase equal to the rise in the cost of living. They seek, and rightly so, a greater share of the gross national product and of the standard of living that their labour makes possible. To say to our people who are over 65 that they must be satisfied with just the same basket of goods and services that they were able to buy at the age of 65 is putting them in a category that is inferior to other people in our society.
The cost of living increases are always behind anyway, but even if they were kept up to date it is putting these people in an inferior position, and to say to them that this additional opportunity to draw unemployment insurance, if they are still working after 65 and meet the conditions of the act, is cut off is I say, grossly unfair. My feeling about the whole matter is that these arguments that are being put forward are not the real arguments. What the government has looked at is the figures and it sees that here is a chance to save more than $100 million a year by cutting off people between the ages of 65 and 70.
In other words, the same thing I have complained about with respect to the other points I mentioned applies here. The government sees itself in trouble about unemployment insurance. It has been under some pressure from its own people, heavily from the Conservatives and to some extent from the public. It sees this program only in terms of trying to save dollars, so it is going to save dollars by doubling the period of disqualification, by lowering to 66 % per cent the benefits to persons with dependants, by making workers pay more by going up from 4 per cent to the actual rate of unemployment before it pays the cost out of general revenue, and then, if that is not enough, by making old people between 65 and 70 literally kick in over $100 million a year by being denied their benefits under this legislation.
That is what we dislike about this legislation. We are concerned. As I said in the bit of history I indulged in a few moments ago, we have been interested in unemployment insurance for a long, long time and we regard it as an important part of our economic and social structure. We do not like seeing it abused by the kinds of things which are being done to it in this amending bill which is now before the House.
The effort to save money by taking it out of the pockets of old people or by taking it out of the pockets of depend-

ants by cutting down what workers with dependants will get is, of course, all based on the notion that somehow the government is being efficient and doing the right thing if it just saves money. To hear some of the speeches in this House one would think that for governments to spend money is a sin. I suggest that if it were not for the collecting and spending of money in the provision of services, pensions and health care, and contributions to housing and unemployment insurance, we would not have a society. There can be no civilization unless we find ways of redistributing the wealth we are able to create so that our people share in the benefits of that society.
That is what a program like unemployment insurance is all about. It needs to be policed; it needs to be administered efficiently and carefully. Above all, it needs to be administered on the basis of fairness. But I resent the way in which the minister and his colleagues seem to have felt that they had to respond to this "save money" syndrome which we get mainly from those on my right. What is important is that the money which is collected and spent in our society results in meeting the needs of our people. That is not done by debasing the unemployment insurance scheme or by making the little people suffer, as is the case under Bill C-69. That is why when the vote on second reading is called, we shall be voting no.

Until the day we reach the Valhalla that the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge and some others have described, and resolve the rationalization of all income support systems and social security systems in this country, until we devise a system of moving on to a pension plan and integrating all these things, I tell you as a minister who has had lots of scars on his back over the last three years, also having had the opportunity to meet with people in Britain, Germany, France, the United States and Sweden, that we have one of the best unemployment insurance plans in the world. It has provided direct cash in almost every instance. It has given very much needed income to people who through no fault of their own suffered an interruption in their earnings at a rate in excess of 2 million people a year since the changes in 1971.
I have heard accusations and criticisms to the effect that I referred to one of the beneficial effects of our plan by saying that it does have a redistributive effect. I make no apology for having said that. If you think it out, it is
November 5, 1975

ridiculous to expect, if it is any good at all, that it would have any other effect. A person who has lost his or her job and therefore their income is, in the main, on the way to becoming very poor. If, through whatever method, you place income in his or her hands, then of course you are redistributing income. What is wrong with that? I think it is unthought-out rhetoric to make accusations that that is a logical or acceptable criticism of the plan that we enjoy in this country.
I would not be a party to emasculation of the unemployment insurance plan as we now have it, at least until that great day comes when we find a much more comprehensive, all-embracing program about which some suggestions have been made in the debate thus far. They are so embryonic, however, that we have a lot of work to do, perhaps together, to perfect the ideas over the years.
I think it is a great plan, but I think the pendulum has perhaps swung a little too far. I cannot stand before you and say it is perfect; there are problems. It is a costly allocation of resources, and even in this still very fortunate country there is not a bottomless pit of money. We have to decide whether this investment in people, as compared to that one, is producing the better or the worse result. There are rigidities in this act that have to be removed. We are trying to do that. I have indicated to the House that I hope to bring forward further improvements and amendments because it is a very significant plan in our society, our economy, and in the allocation of resources required to support it.
I am afraid there are some disincentives in the act and I think they should be attended to. In some of the amendments before the House today we are attempting to deal with these matters. I think we should be extremely careful, though, about using words like "cheater" or "abuse". I am not just playing semantic games. I spent many hours searching my soul about this so that we could understand each other and what really takes place. The person who voluntarily quits with or without cause-and we are addressing ourselves quite heavily to him in this bill-is not in any . legal sense violating the terms of the act. He is making a personal choice which is his right. Having made it, however, that does not automatically entitle him to assume an income paid for by other people.
In regard to disentitlements, people often ask what the percentage is of cheaters or people who misuse the plan. I prefer the term "misuse" because in the main it is applicable to most of the failures to meet the obligations under the act. I think most of it is misuse and a lot of it is misunderstanding because it is a far too complex legal document. It is very difficult to get the basis for assessment of that percentage. A disentitlement could be for one day-it could be for one hour. Well, that is a little tough. The computer would blow a gasket figuring out the deductions in that case. But it can be one day, one week, one month. Disqualifications are precise-they are for a period of time and are usually for reasons that you all know- anyone who voluntarily quits without cause, refusal of suitable work and so on. Indeed the same claimant can be disqualified in the first place and then disentitled later but I defy anyone to tell me precisely what the percentage is.
Having said all that, the incidence of misuse of the plan and even in some cases abuse of the plan, is too high for my
Unemployment Insurance Act
liking. We want to protect the integrity of the program in the eyes of the public of Canada who, after all, is paying for it. I say this because even at present levels of unemployment most Canadians who are capable of working, thank goodness, are enjoying a job. We are, in all conscience, maintaining a vigilant attitude and constantly reviewing that aspect as vigorously as we continue to review our ability to provide services to claimants who need them.
Let me talk more specifically about some of the amendments and controversial provisions contained in Bill C-69. The question arises, how is the program to be paid for? In all probability we are heading for expenditures of about $3.4 billion this year because, thank goodness, unemployment in the last quarter is not climbing. Unquestionably, that is a large amount of money, a large amount of federal government and therefore public expenditure, and a sizable percentage of the gross national product.
The facts are as many hon. members have said, and I do not deny them. In the main, the reason for that figure is that unemployment is at present levels. That is the main reason for the increase in cost. Another reason is that built into the plan is the escalator of the average wage, which determines insurable earnings and, therefore, maximum benefits. The maximum insurable earnings will be $200 per week in 1976, up from the present $185 per week. So there are many built-in cost escalations; in many ways I say thank goodness. But this poses a question which really needs simple arithmetic for its solution.
If you are paying out more money, you have to take in more money. We had to raise more money to fund this plan for 1976 and, perhaps, the future. So it became a question- and I heard some most interesting comments on it-of whether this should be paid completely out of general taxes or whether the program should be maintained by tripartite payments. We chose the route of continuing with the premiums of the employee and employer, with the government sharing the cost. We altered the threshold to allow us to assess more realistically the unemployment situation of the last eight years. The threshold figure for 1976 is to be 5.6 per cent which is based on the eight-year moving average ending last June.
Much has been made of this being a regressive tax, Mr. Speaker, of this being another horrible burden brutally perpetrated on the working people of this country by the Liberal government. Let us get this in perspective. The premium will be paid by nine million employees, by working people whose incomes range from the very modest to the maximum insurable earnings of $200 per week in 1976, and by employers who will pay 1.4 times the employee premium. That means that 58 per cent of the additional $490 million to which I referred, that being the premium revenue increase for 1976, or $280-odd million, will be borne by employers, not employees.
Let me explain to hon. members exactly what this means. The present unemployment insurance premium, at $1.40 per $100 a week income based on a 40-hour week, cost the employee 3.5 cents an hour. Under the new threshold, the increase for that employee, once this bill receives passage, in 1976 will be 25 cents per week on $100 of

earnings. For that same employee the additional cost will be six-tenths of one cent per hour. That is the increase in premium we are talking about. It will be 25 cents a week, or $13 a year. The employer of that same employee who is earning $100 per week in a 40-hour week will pay an increased premium of nine-tenths of one cent per hour for that employee.
Let us consider how this will affect the employee earning the maximum insurable earnings of $200 per week which, as I have just indicated, will be the figure for 1976. The $200 per week, 40-hour week employee will see an increase of a little over one cent per hour in the premium he must pay, and his employer will see an increase of 1.7 cents per hour in the premium that he must pay. So although the principle may be arguable, let us not exaggerate that this is deliberately loading an unconscionable burden on the backs of employees and employers.
For years in this country we have funded unemployment insurance on a tripartite basis, whereby the cost was shared by the three main participants, the employer, employee and the government. Before 1971, the portions of the burden were 41.5 per cent each for the employee and the employer and only 17 per cent for the government, with the government paying the cost of administration. Had we continued at the 4 per cent threshold level, at an unemployment rate similar to that which we experienced in 1975, the shares borne by the government, employer and employee would be, in 1976, 53 per cent for the government, 27 per cent for employer and 20 per cent for employee. The threshold changed, but this does not take the government off the hook financially. It merely restores the balance and, at the new eight-year moving average threshold, the respective shares of the burden would be 38 per cent, 36 per cent and 26 per cent.
Insurable earnings, as I indicated earlier, are indexed to the average industrial wage as collated from T-4 slips. They rise with the increase in earnings, and they also are affected by a moving average. So, Mr. Speaker, I really cannot buy the idea that the government is to be relieved of any concern and that the bureaucrats will say, "To hell with unemployment; we don't have to worry about it any more." How realistic is the suggestion that the government will not remain totally conscious of the burden of unemployment and will not do its best to fight it?

Concern has been expressed about the increased disincentives which we are proposing to apply to those who voluntarily quit their jobs without just cause, who are fired for misconduct or who refuse suitable work. I am concerned about an anomaly, a paradox to do with the present unemployment situation. Despite present levels of unemployment, leaving aside the numbers of existing job openings, there is a continued increase in the numbers of people who leave their jobs without just cause. That number exceeds 250,000 a year. When you consider that number as a percentage of the total claim load-which is a sensible relationship-you will see that it is in excess of 10 per cent. Somebody said that it is only 2 per cent of the work force. Mr. Speaker, 41 per cent of Canadian workers change jobs every year. We are not talking about the right to change jobs. I am talking in terms of 250,000, plus,

people who have attracted disqualifications under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and in those cases no appeals were rescinded.

On the question of jurisprudence, I worry too, from time to time, as to how well our appeal system is working. The jurisprudence has been established for 30 years, though, and if there is valid criticism of this kind of change it should more properly be addressed to an examination of the appeal system itself. I have asked the Unemployment Advisory Committee to conduct a review of the appeal system over the summer months. It really has not been touched for 30 years. It is the subject of an examination, also, by the Law Reform Commission and I hope that before too long we shall either validate it or make necessary corrections. I think we shall find that there is a little rust in it; it needs to be brought up to date; it needs a better balance, particularly for the unorganized worker who faces a negative decision.
I turn now to the position of those over 65. This is the most difficult problem I had to wrestle with and place before members. I want to begin by asking hon. members by what stretch of the imagination can one visualize that this change is suggesting that people aged 65 and over be barred from work? There is nothing whatsoever in this change in entitlement which will affect a person's right to work, or access to work. It simply means that unemployment insurance, in my opinion and in the opinion of many others, is not a program designed to provide even a shortterm pension plan. I admire the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for his unrelenting effort to assist senior citizens. I question the route he takes very often, because I think it would lead to very severe distortions, crippling one plan by requiring resources which should more properly be allocated to another.

They had the choice of taking three weeks' benefits or the Canada Pension Plan. Obviously, they decided not to go that silly route under the act because it wasn't very profitable for them. We are dealing here with $120 million a year.
There is a matter here which I am bound to take into consideration. It is this. We have extrapolated from the labour force survey the people aged 65 and over who tell the survey that they are unemployed. We have compared that figure with the number of unemployment insurance claimants at any given time, and the comparison is startling, I am sad to say. The labour force survey indicated that the average monthly number of those aged 65 or over, unemployed in 1974, was 7,000. The average number of claimants aged 65 and over was 17,500. It ranged to a ratio of 5,000 unemployed but 18,000 drawing unemployment insurance benefits, to that average. I will give hon. members who are interested more details when we reach committee stage, but that is the problem.

Unemployment Insurance Act
Before we get into committee I want to give hon. members our forecast of the financial implications of these amendments in terms of the benefits paid. The disqualification change we rate at a savings of $80 million. I am basing this on a 7 per cent unemployment rate, somewhat comparable to the rate this year. It would fluctuate in accordance with whatever unemployment rate we experience. The sickness benefit, increased flexibility, represents an additional cost of $15 million. The change in the qualifying and benefit period will mean an additional $15 million-that is a cost increase-and the change in the dependency rate represents a reduction of $30 million. The change in the provision respecting those 65 years of age and over represents a saving of $120 million.
